REMOVAL OF A TRUSTEE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust · March 14, 2020

PURPOSE OF THIS REMOVAL OF A TRUSTEE INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes the California statutory framework governing removal of a trustee, as background in connection with The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust, executed March 14, 2020, for which Jordan Alex Lee serves or has been asked to serve as trustee and Morgan Lee is referenced as a successor for identification only. Jordan Alex Lee's children, in equal shares and Jordan Lee are likewise referenced for identification only, and any reference to Sacramento County or CGC-26-123456 identifies where and under what number a removal proceeding may be or has been filed. This document covers the statutory grounds on which a court may remove a trustee, who may seek removal and by what pathways, the court's own-motion authority to remove an unlicensed professional fiduciary, the circumstances that create a vacancy in the office of trustee, and the cost-shifting and interim-protection rules that apply while a removal petition is pending. It does not itself remove any trustee, does not itself constitute a petition filed with any court, and does not evaluate whether grounds for removal exist for Jordan Alex Lee or any other trustee of The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust or any other trust. This is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about a specific trustee's removal.

THREE PATHWAYS BY WHICH A TRUSTEE MAY BE REMOVED
California Probate Code § 15642(a) identifies three distinct pathways by which a trustee of The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust may be removed from office: in accordance with a removal mechanism the trust instrument itself provides, by the court acting on its own motion, or on a petition filed under Probate Code § 17200 by a settlor, a cotrustee, or a beneficiary. These pathways are not mutually exclusive, and the statute does not require that a trust instrument address removal at all before the other two pathways become available. Probate Code § 17200(b)(10) separately confirms that appointing or removing a trustee, and § 17200(b)(11) accepting a trustee's resignation, are among the purposes for which a petition concerning a trust's internal affairs may be brought.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A trustee may be removed in accordance with the trust instrument, by the court on its own motion, or on petition of a settlor, cotrustee, or beneficiary under Section 17200."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(a) (California Legislative Information text), the three pathways by which a trustee may be removed: per the trust instrument, by the court's own motion, or on petition under Section 17200 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15642.)
  "(10) Appointing or removing a trustee. (11) Accepting the resignation of a trustee."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 17200(b)(10)-(11) (California Legislative Information text), appointing or removing a trustee, and accepting a trustee's resignation, as listed purposes of a Section 17200 petition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=17200.)
  Known gap: Section 15642(a) does not itself specify a filing fee, a required notice period, or the form of a petition brought under Section 17200; those procedural requirements come from other Probate Code sections, the Judicial Council forms, and the California Rules of Court, none of which this clause reproduces.

GENERAL STATUTORY GROUNDS FOR COURT-ORDERED REMOVAL
Probate Code § 15642(b) lists the grounds on which a court may remove a trustee. Apart from the disqualified-person ground addressed separately in this document, those grounds include a breach of trust, insolvency or other unfitness to administer the trust, hostility or lack of cooperation among cotrustees that impairs administration, a trustee's failure or decline to act, and compensation that is excessive under the circumstances. The statute also lists a trustee's substantial inability — as determined under Probate Code Division 2, Part 17 (commencing with § 810) — to manage the trust's financial resources or otherwise properly execute the duties of the office, a trustee's substantial inability to resist fraud or undue influence, and, as a catch-all, 'other good cause.' For a trustee who holds the power to revoke the trust, the statute specifies that substantial inability to manage financial resources or to resist fraud or undue influence may not be proved solely by isolated incidents of negligence or improvidence.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(b) The grounds for removal of a trustee by the court include the following: (1) Where the trustee has committed a breach of the trust. (2) Where the trustee is insolvent or otherwise unfit to administer the trust. (3) Where hostility or lack of cooperation among cotrustees impairs the administration of the trust. (4) Where the trustee fails or declines to act. (5) Where the trustee’s compensation is excessive under the circumstances."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(b)(1)-(5) (California Legislative Information text), breach of trust, insolvency/unfitness, cotrustee hostility, failure to act, and excessive compensation as removal grounds (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15642.)
  "(7) If, as determined under Part 17 (commencing with Section 810) of Division 2, the trustee is substantially unable to manage the trust’s financial resources or is otherwise substantially unable to execute properly the duties of the office. When the trustee holds the power to revoke the trust, substantial inability to manage the trust’s financial resources or otherwise execute properly the duties of the office may not be proved solely by isolated incidents of negligence or improvidence. (8) If the trustee is substantially unable to resist fraud or undue influence. When the trustee holds the power to revoke the trust, substantial inability to resist fraud or undue influence may not be proved solely by isolated incidents of negligence or improvidence. (9) For other good cause."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(b)(7)-(9) (California Legislative Information text), substantial inability to manage trust resources or execute duties, substantial inability to resist fraud or undue influence, and 'other good cause' as removal grounds (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15642.)
  Known gap: The statute states these as grounds a court may act on; it does not itself define terms such as 'unfit to administer the trust' or 'excessive' compensation, does not guarantee that removal will be ordered whenever a listed ground is shown, and does not address how these grounds interact with a no-contest clause or an exculpatory provision that a particular trust instrument might contain.

REMOVAL GROUND FOR A SOLE TRUSTEE WHO IS A DISQUALIFIED PERSON
Probate Code § 15642(b)(6) provides a distinct removal ground where the sole trustee of The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust is a person described in Probate Code § 21380(a) — the categories of persons (including an instrument's drafter, a fiduciary who transcribed it, and certain care custodians) to whom a donative transfer is separately presumed the product of fraud or undue influence — regardless of whether that person is also the transferee of a donative transfer under the instrument. This removal ground does not apply if the court finds, based on evidence of the settlor's intent and all other facts and circumstances, that it is consistent with the settlor's intent for the trustee to continue serving and that this intent was not the product of fraud or undue influence, subject to three narrower statutory exceptions concerning family or cohabitant relationships, a signed Certificate of Independent Review, or court approval under a conservatorship-transfer procedure. For purposes of this ground, 'related by blood or marriage' includes persons within the seventh degree, and any waiver by the settlor of the ground itself is against public policy and void. The paragraph does not apply to instruments that became irrevocable on or before January 1, 1994.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(6) Where the sole trustee is a person described in subdivision (a) of Section 21380, whether or not the person is the transferee of a donative transfer by the transferor, unless, based upon any evidence of the intent of the settlor and all other facts and circumstances, which shall be made known to the court, the court finds that it is consistent with the settlor’s intent that the trustee continue to serve and that this intent was not the product of fraud or undue influence. Any waiver by the settlor of this provision is against public policy and shall be void."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(b)(6) (California Legislative Information text), the removal ground applicable to a sole trustee described in Section 21380(a), and the settlor-intent finding that displaces it absent statutory exceptions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15642.)
  "For purposes of this section, the term “related by blood or marriage” shall include persons within the seventh degree."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(f) (California Legislative Information text), the definition of 'related by blood or marriage' for purposes of the removal statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15642.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the operative sentence of paragraph (6) and the definitional subdivision (f); it does not reproduce the full text of the three exceptions in subparagraphs (A)-(C) of paragraph (6), including the exact wording required for a Certificate of Independent Review, nor the separate donative-transfer presumption in Probate Code § 21380 itself, which this corpus addresses in its Disqualified-Transferee Donative Transfer Presumption information sheet as a distinct question from removal from the office of trustee.

COURT'S OWN-MOTION AUTHORITY TO REMOVE AN UNLICENSED PROFESSIONAL FIDUCIARY TRUSTEE
Probate Code § 17200(c) gives the court an own-motion basis to question a trustee's continued service that is independent of the grounds listed in § 15642(b). Under that subdivision, the court may set and give notice of an order to show cause why a trustee who is a professional fiduciary required to be licensed under Business and Professions Code § 6500 et seq. should not be removed for failing to hold a valid, unexpired, unsuspended license. This authority does not require a settlor, cotrustee, or beneficiary to file a petition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The court may, on its own motion, set and give notice of an order to show cause why a trustee who is a professional fiduciary, and who is required to be licensed under Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 6500) of Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code, should not be removed for failing to hold a valid, unexpired, unsuspended license."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 17200(c) (California Legislative Information text), the court's own-motion authority to set an order to show cause why an unlicensed professional fiduciary trustee should not be removed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=17200.)
  Known gap: Section 17200(c) authorizes but does not require the court to act on its own motion, does not itself define 'professional fiduciary' or reproduce the licensing requirements of Business and Professions Code § 6500 et seq., and does not address removal of a professional fiduciary trustee on any ground other than an unlicensed status.

CIRCUMSTANCES THAT CREATE A VACANCY IN THE OFFICE OF TRUSTEE
Probate Code § 15643 identifies eight circumstances under which a vacancy exists in the office of trustee of The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust: the person named as trustee rejects the trust; the person named as trustee cannot be identified or does not exist; the trustee resigns or is removed; the trustee dies; a conservator or guardian of the person or estate of an individual trustee is appointed; the trustee is the subject of an order for relief in bankruptcy; a trust company's charter is revoked or its powers suspended for 30 days or more; or a receiver is appointed for a trust company and the appointment is not vacated within 30 days. A trustee's removal under § 15642 is therefore only one of several statutory events that can create a vacancy that must then be filled.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "There is a vacancy in the office of trustee in any of the following circumstances: (a) The person named as trustee rejects the trust. (b) The person named as trustee cannot be identified or does not exist. (c) The trustee resigns or is removed. (d) The trustee dies. (e) A conservator or guardian of the person or estate of an individual trustee is appointed. (f) The trustee is the subject of an order for relief in bankruptcy. (g) A trust company’s charter is revoked or powers are suspended, if the revocation or suspension is to be in effect for a period of 30 days or more. (h) A receiver is appointed for a trust company if the appointment is not vacated within a period of 30 days."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15643 (California Legislative Information text), the eight circumstances that create a vacancy in the office of trustee (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15643.)
  Known gap: Section 15643 identifies when a vacancy exists but does not itself address how a vacancy is filled once it arises, does not specify any deadline by which a vacancy must be filled, and does not by itself suspend trust administration during the vacancy — how a vacancy created by any of these eight circumstances is filled is governed separately by Probate Code § 15660, which is not reproduced in this document because this corpus already addresses it, with a byte-verified quotation, in the Revocable Living Trust document's 'Filling a Vacancy in the Office of Trustee' clause.

COST-SHIFTING RULES TIED TO A REMOVAL PROCEEDING
Probate Code § 15642 ties an award of costs and attorney's fees to two specific findings made in a removal proceeding, rather than creating a general fee-shifting rule for every removal petition. Under subdivision (c), if the court finds — in connection with the disqualified-person ground in paragraph (6) of subdivision (b) — that the trustee's designation was not consistent with the settlor's intent or was the product of fraud or undue influence, the trustee being removed bears all costs of the proceeding, including reasonable attorney's fees. Under subdivision (d), if the court instead finds that a petition for removal was filed in bad faith and that removal would be contrary to the settlor's intent, the court may order that the person or persons who sought removal bear all or part of the proceeding's costs, including reasonable attorney's fees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If, pursuant to paragraph (6) of subdivision (b), the court finds that the designation of the trustee was not consistent with the intent of the settlor or was the product of fraud or undue influence, the person being removed as trustee shall bear all costs of the proceeding, including reasonable attorney’s fees."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(c) (California Legislative Information text), fee-shifting against the trustee on a finding under the disqualified-person ground in paragraph (6) of subdivision (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15642.)
  "If the court finds that the petition for removal of the trustee was filed in bad faith and that removal would be contrary to the settlor’s intent, the court may order that the person or persons seeking the removal of the trustee bear all or any part of the costs of the proceeding, including reasonable attorney’s fees."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(d) (California Legislative Information text), fee-shifting against a petitioner on a finding that a removal petition was filed in bad faith and contrary to the settlor's intent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15642.)
  Known gap: Subdivisions (c) and (d) each shift fees only on the specific findings described; the statute does not create any general fee-shifting rule for a removal proceeding brought on the other grounds listed in subdivision (b), where each side otherwise bears its own attorney's fees under the general California rule absent some other statutory or trust-instrument basis for shifting them.

INTERIM PROTECTION OF TRUST PROPERTY WHILE A REMOVAL PETITION IS PENDING
Probate Code § 15642(e) addresses the period between the filing of a removal petition concerning The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust and the court's decision, including any appellate review. If it appears to the court that trust property or a beneficiary's interests may suffer loss or injury during that period, the court — on its own motion or on petition of a cotrustee or beneficiary — may compel the trustee whose removal is sought to surrender trust property to a cotrustee, a receiver, or a temporary trustee, and may suspend the trustee's powers to the extent the court deems necessary.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If it appears to the court that trust property or the interests of a beneficiary may suffer loss or injury pending a decision on a petition for removal of a trustee and any appellate review, the court may, on its own motion or on petition of a cotrustee or beneficiary, compel the trustee whose removal is sought to surrender trust property to a cotrustee or to a receiver or temporary trustee. The court may also suspend the powers of the trustee to the extent the court deems necessary."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(e) (California Legislative Information text), the court's authority to compel surrender of trust property to a cotrustee, receiver, or temporary trustee, and to suspend the trustee's powers, pending decision on a removal petition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15642.)
  Known gap: Section 15642(e) authorizes this interim relief 'to the extent the court deems necessary' but does not itself specify a standard of proof, a required showing of irreparable harm, or a procedure such as an ex parte application for seeking the relief before a full hearing on removal; those procedural mechanics are not addressed in this section and are not reproduced here.

citations.cite: the court's authority to compel surrender of trust property to a cotrustee, receiver, or temporary trustee, and to suspend the trustee's powers, pending decision on a removal petition
citations.quote: If it appears to the court that trust property or the interests of a beneficiary may suffer loss or injury pending a decision on a petition for removal of a trustee and any appellate review, the court may, on its own motion or on petition of a cotrustee or beneficiary, compel the trustee whose removal is sought to surrender trust property to a cotrustee or to a receiver or temporary trustee. The court may also suspend the powers of the trustee to the extent the court deems necessary.

expectedJSON.gap: Section 15642(e) authorizes this interim relief 'to the extent the court deems necessary' but does not itself specify a standard of proof, a required showing of irreparable harm, or a procedure such as an ex parte application for seeking the relief before a full hearing on removal; those procedural mechanics are not addressed in this section and are not reproduced here.
